planting.note: Plant offshoots or tissue-cultured trees in spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Deglet Noor needs a long, hot, dry summer to properly ripen its fruit and is best suited to low-humidity desert climates.

directions: Plant offshoots or tissue-cultured trees in spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Deglet Noor needs a long, hot, dry summer to properly ripen its fruit and is best suited to low-humidity desert climates. Known as the 'light of the date' for its translucent amber color when held to the light, this semi-dry cultivar is the most widely grown commercial date variety in the United States, historically the backbone of California's Coachella Valley date industry after being introduced from Algeria in the early twentieth century, prized for a firm, chewy texture and balanced, not-too-sweet flavor that holds up well in baking and storage. Like all date palms it requires an extremely long, hot, arid growing season to properly cure and sweeten its fruit on the tree, making it poorly suited to humid climates where fruit is prone to souring or fermenting before it fully ripens. Female trees need a nearby male date palm or hand-pollination to produce fruit, and expect several years of growth before the tree reaches bearing maturity.

An Iraqi soft date variety highly prized for being one of the very few dates good to eat fresh at the crisp, yellow, apple-like khalal stage rather than only after fully drying to the traditional wrinkled brown tamr stage, giving it a uniquely refreshing, crunchy-sweet quality unlike most commercial dried dates. Once fully ripened to the soft, caramel-brown stage it becomes exceptionally sweet and soft with a rich, almost butterscotch flavor, making it a favorite among date connoisseurs for both fresh and fully cured eating. Like all date palms it demands a long, hot, dry growing season to ripen properly, needs a male pollinator tree or hand pollination for fruit set, and requires many years of growth before reaching bearing maturity.

planting.note: Plant container-grown palms in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; footstool palm is frost-tender and grown as an indoor or greenhouse palm outside zones 10-11.

directions: Plant container-grown palms in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; footstool palm is frost-tender and grown as an indoor or greenhouse palm outside zones 10-11. Distinctive round, pleated, fan-shaped leaves give this Southeast Asian palm both its common name and a soft, almost circular silhouette unlike the more angular fan shape of many other fan palms, with a slender trunk that grows quickly and gracefully upward once established. Popular as a young potted palm for interior spaces due to its attractive round leaf shape and relatively fast juvenile growth, it eventually becomes a substantial landscape tree in frost-free tropical climates far too large for typical indoor culture. Water when the top of the potting mix or soil begins to dry, provide bright indirect light or filtered outdoor shade, and protect from any frost, since the species has essentially no cold tolerance.

planting.note: Plant container-grown palms in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in full sun; Cuban royal palm is frost-tender and realistic outdoors only in the warmest parts of zones 10-11.

directions: Plant container-grown palms in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in full sun; Cuban royal palm is frost-tender and realistic outdoors only in the warmest parts of zones 10-11. National tree of Cuba and one of the most iconic and widely planted ornamental palms in the tropics and subtropics, it develops a smooth, strikingly white to gray, columnar trunk topped with a distinctive green crownshaft and a full, arching crown of feathery fronds, a stately, formal silhouette long used to line grand boulevards and estate driveways across South Florida, the Caribbean, and other frost-free regions. Closely related to and sometimes confused with the Florida royal palm native to the Everglades, it grows quickly in warm, humid, fertile conditions into a truly massive, single-trunk specimen, making it a tree only for large properties with ample vertical and horizontal space. Water regularly, especially while young, feed with a palm-specific fertilizer to prevent common nutrient deficiencies, and protect young palms from any frost, since the species has very little cold tolerance.

planting.note: Plant container-grown cycads in spring in well-drained, average soil in partial shade to full sun; Prince Sago tolerates more cold and grows notably faster than the common sago palm, but still needs protection from hard freezes when young.

directions: Plant container-grown cycads in spring in well-drained, average soil in partial shade to full sun; Prince Sago tolerates more cold and grows notably faster than the common sago palm, but still needs protection from hard freezes when young. Closely related to and often confused with the ubiquitous sago palm (Cycas revoluta), this Taiwanese cycad grows considerably faster and develops a taller, more slender trunk with a fuller, more graceful crown of glossy, dark green, feathery fronds, making it an increasingly popular alternative where a bigger, quicker-growing cycad specimen is wanted. Like all cycads it is an ancient, primitive plant lineage predating flowering plants, tolerant of poor soil and drought once established, and slow enough overall that a young specimen still represents a significant long-term investment despite its faster relative growth rate. Water sparingly once established, protect young plants from hard freezes with covering during cold snaps, and avoid overwatering, which is the most common cause of root and stem rot in cycads.
